Developing nations face a dual challenge: expanding access to electricity while limiting carbon emissions. For decades, fossil fuels dominated their energy mix, but the falling cost of solar and wind technology has begun to change this picture dramatically. Solar power, in particular, has emerged as a game-changer. In many rural regions where extending the traditional grid is prohibitively expensive, small solar installations now bring light to homes that had never before been connected. These decentralised systems are often cheaper and quicker to deploy than large power plants. Yet the transition is far from (I). Financing remains a major obstacle, as upfront costs deter households and small businesses. Governments in poorer countries frequently lack the capital to subsidise clean energy on the scale required, and international funding, though growing, is still inadequate. Policy also plays a crucial role. Nations that have offered stable incentives and clear regulations have attracted far more investment than those with unpredictable rules. Political will, therefore, can be as important as technology in determining the pace of adoption. Despite these hurdles, the momentum appears unstoppable. As prices continue to decline and awareness of climate risks grows, renewable energy is likely to become the default choice rather than a costly alternative for the developing world.
